reading.rtitle: Room 4: The Care of Others -- room text and label
paras: Room 4: The Care of Others. The five works in this room were made between 2016 and 2024 by artists whose practice sits between contemporary art and clinical research. At the centre of the room is a large-scale site-specific sound installation built from recordings made in a public hospital; around it hang four small untitled works on paper, lent by the artist. The room takes its title from a phrase that recurs in the literature on the care of the chronically ill, and it asks a single question: what happens to a person's story once an institution writes it down?

A wall label is a compressed argument, and every word in it has been fought over. The label for the sound installation reads: Untitled (Ward 7), 2023. Mixed media: four-channel sound, hospital furniture, printed transcripts. Dimensions variable. Courtesy of the artist and a private collection. On loan until March. Nine facts in six lines, and not one adjective. The interpretation team writes the room text; the registrar writes the label; and the artist is asked to approve the medium line, because that is the line artists most often want changed.

Two of the works on paper were acquired by the museum in 2019, and the label records that in three words: Acquisition, 2019, gift. The other two are attributed to the same artist but not signed, and the label says so in one word, because provenance for work made inside a hospital is rarely complete. Visitors read a label for about eight seconds. A room text gets perhaps thirty. Everything the institution wants to say about a work has to survive that, which is why the sentences here are short and the noun phrases are long.

The medium line should read mixed media, not installation.

Courtesy of the artist and the gallery, with the city after the gallery name.
It is an untitled work, and the label should keep the capital U.

listenings.text: This is the part of the job that nobody outside the building knows exists. A label looks like a set of facts, and half of it is a decision. We have about sixty words for a room text and about twenty for a label, and every one of them is negotiated. The medium line is where it usually gets difficult. An artist will write, quite reasonably, that the work is a sound piece about a hospital, and we have to turn that into mixed media, four-channel sound, hospital furniture, printed transcripts, because a label describes what is in the room, not what the work is about. What the work is about goes in the room text, and the room text is a different genre entirely. My advice to any artist who is about to be shown for the first time is very simple. Ask to see the label before it is printed, and read the medium line out loud. If it does not sound like your work, say so that week, because once it is on the wall it stays there for the whole run of the show.

A quick word about the two lines at the bottom of the label, the ones visitors skip and researchers read first. The credit line tells you how the work got here. Courtesy of the artist means it came straight from the studio and goes straight back to it. On loan, with a date after it, means it belongs to somebody else and we have it for a fixed period, and when that date passes the wall goes empty until we hang something else. Acquisition, with a year after it, means it is ours and it is not going anywhere. The second line is the provenance, which is the ownership history, and it is only ever as good as the paperwork. For work made in the last ten years it is usually complete. For anything older, or anything made inside an institution like a hospital or a school, there are gaps, and we write attributed to rather than by when we cannot prove the hand. That one word is the difference between a certainty and a strong argument, and it is not a small thing to put on a wall.
